newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Exiles say China executes five Uighur rioters.
newsitem.headline: Exiles say China executes five Uighur rioters.

text.p: An exile group said on Monday that China had executed five ethnic Uighurs who were accused of involvement in riots that rocked the country's predominantly Moslem northwest province of Xinjiang last month.

"We know for sure that five people (Uighurs) were executed on March 20," Mukhiddin Mukhlisi, spokesman for the United National Revolutionary Front of East Turkestan, said at a congress of exile Uighur groups near the Kazakh capital Almaty.
Officials in Xinjiang said last week they had indicted six people, who could face the death penalty if convicted, in connection with anti-Chinese rioting in the province.
But they denied allegations made by exiled Uighur separatists that China would execute two rioters.
Mukhlisi told Reuters the executions took place in the town of Yining, located near the Chinese-Kazakh border and scene of last month's disturbances which left nine dead and 198 wounded.
A western traveller recently returned from the region said Yining was now calm.
But he added security was tight across Xinjiang province: "There are Chinese soldiers virtually everywhere you go."

Mukhlisi named one of those executed as Abdukhalil Abdulmedchit, saying he was a prominent leader of the rioting, but he could not name the other four. He said the two names he gave last week of two students facing execution were incorrect.
Information from the vast but closed region of mountain and hostile desert is difficult to verify. News often arrives days late from traders crossing the busy China-Kazakh border.
The Front is one of several Uighur organisations fighting for an independent "East Turkestan" in Xinjiang, home to a majority of Turkic-speaking Moslems, like the ethnic Uighurs.

Mukhlisi's group and two others -- the Regional Association of Uighurs and the Free Uighuristan movement -- met in the village of Kalinino, 15 km (nine miles) east of Almaty, at a congress aimed at uniting exile groups in Kazakhstan.
About 300 turned out from remote parts of Kazakhstan and neighbouring Kyrgyzstan to attend the congress.

Last year, the Xinjiang authorities cracked down on Uighur secessionists after a series of violent clashes, bombings and assassination attempts on officials and Moslem leaders regarded as pro-Beijing.
Exile groups said last month the Yining riots were sparked by the execution of about 30 Uighurs by the Chinese authorities.
